entries.1603b3f3962284fcb49164649264c88178f8445f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4899"/><div sID="gen7193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4899"/>4. Job's difficulty was not as to man, but as to God, why He so afflicted him, as if he were the guilty hypocrite which the friends alleged him to be. Vulgate translates it, "my disputation."<div eID="gen7193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if it were--</hi>rather, "since this is the case." <div eID="gen7194" type="x-p"/>
entries.56a90226eb744c65a97320cc2f3c0b60a25a430c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4900"/><div sID="gen7195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4900"/><hi type="bold">5. lay ... hand upon ... mouth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Pr 30:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.18.19">Jud 18:19</reference>). So the heathen god of silence was pictured with his hand on his mouth. There was enough in Job's case to awe them into silence (<reference osisRef="Job.17.8">Job 17:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7195" type="x-p"/>
entries.9acef9b42269c0a252ab7f86962ed52a95f81edb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4901"/><div sID="gen7196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4901"/><hi type="bold">6. remember--</hi>Think on it. Can you wonder that I broke out into complaints, when the struggle was not with men, but with the Almighty? Reconcile, if you can, the ceaseless woes of the innocent with the divine justice! Is it not enough to make one tremble? [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7196" type="x-p"/>
entries.db5edb09811068315329817b90f41e9ba47fdc7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4902"/><div sID="gen7197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4902"/>7. The answer is <reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Ro 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">Psa 73:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11-Eccl.8.13">Ec 8:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Lu 2:35</reference>-end; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pr 16:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Ro 9:22</reference>.<div eID="gen7197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old--</hi>in opposition to the friends who asserted that sinners are "cut off" early (<reference osisRef="Job.8.12">Job 8:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen7198" type="x-p"/>
entries.33b37d8facd21765ef0c7a7497596befe62a43f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4903"/><div sID="gen7199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4903"/>8. In opposition to <reference osisRef="Job.18.19">Job 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.4">5:4</reference>. <div eID="gen7199" type="x-p"/>
entries.0abf7e1a7669cd03f3daaec2137de376e5469532: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4904"/><div sID="gen7200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4904"/>9. Literally, "peace from fear"; with poetic force. Their house is peace itself, far removed from fear. Opposed to the friends' assertion, as to the bad (Job 15:21-24; 20:26-28), and conversely, the good (<reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job 5:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen7200" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5cf5357129a49a832317ffbd6e7187f7b74f44f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4905"/><div sID="gen7201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4905"/>10. Rather, "their cattle conceive." The first clause of the verse describes an easy conception, the second, a happy birth [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7201" type="x-p"/>
entries.68364374ae827ae00dace01bbb8c6f16b1ea92d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4906"/><div sID="gen7202" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4906"/><hi type="bold">11. send forth--</hi>namely, out of doors, to their happy sports under the skies, like a joyful flock sent to the pastures.<div eID="gen7202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">little ones--</hi>like lambkins.<div eID="gen7203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children--</hi>somewhat older than the former.<div eID="gen7204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dance--</hi>not formal dances; but skip, like lambs, in joyous and healthful play. <div eID="gen7205" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fbb7d08414ddebc1afd305019b2284b93502290: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4907"/><div sID="gen7206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4907"/><hi type="bold">12. take--</hi>rather, "lift up the voice" (sing) to the note of [Umbreit].<div eID="gen7206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">timbrel--</hi>rather, "tambourine."<div eID="gen7207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">organ--</hi>not the modern "organ," but the "pipe" (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.21">Ge 4:21</reference>). The first clause refers to stringed, the latter, to wind instruments; thus, with "the voice" all kinds of music are enumerated. <div eID="gen7208" type="x-p"/>
entries.53e31749424efe035911fa8d589d5e71335f4712: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4908"/><div sID="gen7209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4908"/><hi type="bold">13. wealth--</hi>Old English Version for "prosperity."<div eID="gen7209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a moment--</hi>not by a lingering disease. Great blessings! Lengthened life with prosperity, and a sudden painless death (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.4">Psa 73:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7210" type="x-p"/>
entries.a36971b63d259d739d781def86a9b01e9fedd1ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4909"/><div sID="gen7211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4909"/><hi type="bold">14. Therefore--</hi>rather, "And yet they are such as say," &c., that is, say, not in so many words, but virtually, by their conduct (so the Gergesenes, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.34">Mt 8:34</reference>). How differently the godly (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen7211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ways--</hi>The course of action, which God points out; as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>, Margin. <div eID="gen7212" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a15249d3b707434b344de83813cb11964fbab2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4910"/><div sID="gen7213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4910"/>15. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jr 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pr 30:9</reference>, Margin, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.2">Ex 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen7213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what profit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference>; Mal 3:14; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference>). Sinners ask, not what is right, but what is for the profit of self. They forget, "If religion cost self something, the want of it will cost self infinitely more." <div eID="gen7214" type="x-p"/>
entries.806e11b0a17ed5b135b700721db9db7857bab79d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4911"/><div sID="gen7215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4911"/><hi type="bold">16. not in their hand--</hi>but in the hand of God. This is Job's difficulty, that God who has sinners prosperity (good) in His hand should allow them to have it.<div eID="gen7215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is--</hi>rather, "may the counsel of the wicked be far from me!" [Umbreit]. This naturally follows the sentiment of the first clause: Let me not hereby be thought to regard with aught but horror the ways of the wicked, however prosperous. <div eID="gen7216" type="x-p"/>
entries.09e14a201993365e3dfebb12ccf73544ac194378: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4912"/><div sID="gen7217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4912"/>17. Job in this whole passage down to <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference> quotes the assertion of the friends, as to the short continuance of the sinner's prosperity, not his own sentiments. In <reference osisRef="Job.21.22">Job 21:22</reference> he proceeds to refute them. "How oft is the candle" (lamp), &c., quoting Bildad's sentiment (<reference osisRef="Job.18.5">Job 18:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.6">6</reference>), in order to question its truth (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.8">Mt 25:8</reference>).<div eID="gen7217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how oft--</hi>"God distributeth," &c. (alluding to <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen7218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrows--</hi>Umbreit translates "snares," literally, "cords," which lightning in its twining motion resembles (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>). <div eID="gen7219" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c8e957656837277f1e81558549edf82b124687f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4913"/><div sID="gen7220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4913"/>18. Job alludes to a like sentiment of Bildad (<reference osisRef="Job.18.18">Job 18:18</reference>), using his own previous words (<reference osisRef="Job.13.25">Job 13:25</reference>). <div eID="gen7220" type="x-p"/>
entries.655bf6e1514ddf5dd7463c9c06e758006ddfdefa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4914"/><div sID="gen7221" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4914"/>19. Equally questionable is the friends' assertion that if the godless himself is not punished, the children are (<reference osisRef="Job.18.19">Job 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.10">20:10</reference>); and that God rewardeth him here for his iniquity, and that he shall know it to his cost. So "know" (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Ho 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7221" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc4dba17e859a5e3f1b9fb230d16676dd203aeeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4915"/><div sID="gen7222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4915"/>20. Another questionable assertion of the friends, that the sinner sees his own and his children's destruction in his lifetime.<div eID="gen7222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>). <div eID="gen7223" type="x-p"/>
entries.8015efa175f020420176db7503a3e86e5c29cb47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4916"/><div sID="gen7224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4916"/><hi type="bold">21. The argument of the friends, in proof of <reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference>, What pleasure can he have from his house (children) when he is dead--</hi>("after him," <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>).<div eID="gen7224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when the number, &c.--</hi>Or, rather, "What hath he to do with his children?" &c. (so the Hebrew in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">8:6</reference>). It is therefore necessary that "his eyes should see his and their destruction" (see <reference osisRef="Job.14.21">Job 14:21</reference>).<div eID="gen7225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>rather, when the number of his allotted months is fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Job.14.5">Job 14:5</reference>). From an Arabic word, "arrow," which was used to draw lots with. Hence "arrow"--inevitable destiny [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7226" type="x-p"/>
entries.cce8f24edb44e15bfe9f406d45294fc721f95e19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4917"/><div sID="gen7227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4917"/>22. Reply of Job, "In all these assertions you try to teach God how He ought to deal with men, rather than prove that He does in fact so deal with them. Experience is against you. God gives prosperity and adversity as it pleases Him, not as man's wisdom would have it, on principles inscrutable to us" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Is 40:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Ro 11:34</reference>).<div eID="gen7227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those ... high--</hi>the high ones, not only angels, but men (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.12-Isa.2.17">Is 2:12-17</reference>). <div eID="gen7228" type="x-p"/>
entries.530075f985c3dda708d9e67e3882462642807f05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4918"/><div sID="gen7229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4918"/>23. Literally, "in the bone of his perfection," that is, the full strength of unimpaired prosperity [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7229" type="x-p"/>
entries.096f4a96378d3cae9a769a3e044f1e1a48865a3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4919"/><div sID="gen7230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4919"/><hi type="bold">24. breasts--</hi>rather, "skins," or "vessels" for fluids [Lee]. But [Umbreit] "stations or resting-places of his herds near water"; in opposition to Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>); the first clause refers to his abundant substance, the second to his vigorous health.<div eID="gen7230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">moistened--</hi>comparing man's body to a well-watered field (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pr 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7231" type="x-p"/>
entries.a456851f483de3b9f10cfe62fdf5302d4ba59d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4920"/><div sID="gen7232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4920"/>26. (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Ec 9:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7232" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a411fa16b2da0193fd803adc1797c4150591436: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4921"/><div sID="gen7233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4921"/>27. Their wrongful thoughts against Job are stated by him in <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference>. They do not honestly name Job, but insinuate his guilt. <div eID="gen7233" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b351fd68df0675badeae866c294b1f650e36b18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4922"/><div sID="gen7234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4922"/><hi type="bold">28. ye say--</hi>referring to Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.20.7">Job 20:7</reference>).<div eID="gen7234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the house--</hi>referring to the fall of the house of Job's oldest son (<reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>) and the destruction of his family.<div eID="gen7235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prince--</hi>The parallel "wicked" in the second clause requires this to be taken in a bad sense, tyrant, oppressor (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Is 13:2</reference>), the same Hebrew, "nobles"--oppressors.<div eID="gen7236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelling-places--</hi>rather, "pavilions," a tent containing many dwellings, such as a great emir, like Job, with many dependents, would have. <div eID="gen7237" type="x-p"/>
entries.c29e010321155bc2b5f5e2385ab938514120857f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4923"/><div sID="gen7238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4923"/>29. Job, seeing that the friends will not admit him as an impartial judge, as they consider his calamities prove his guilt, begs them to ask the opinion of travellers (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">La 1:12</reference>), who have the experience drawn from observation, and who are no way connected with him. Job opposes this to Bildad (<reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>) and Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.20.4">Job 20:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tokens--</hi>rather, "intimations" (for example, inscriptions, proverbs, signifying the results of their observation), testimony. Literally, "signs" or proofs in confirmation of the word spoken (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.11">Is 7:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7239" type="x-p"/>
entries.78dd0acba31d32961a88af0a76a90219316f0daf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4924"/><div sID="gen7240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4924"/>30. Their testimony (referring perhaps to those who had visited the region where Abraham who enjoyed a revelation then lived) is that "the wicked is (now) spared (reserved) against the day of destruction (hereafter)." The Hebrew does not so well agree with [Umbreit] "in the day of destruction." Job does not deny sinners' future punishment, but their punishment in this life. They have their "good things" now. Hereafter, their lot, and that of the godly, shall be reversed (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Lu 16:25</reference>). Job, by the Spirit, often utters truths which solve the difficulty under which he labored. His afflictions mostly clouded his faith, else he would have seen the solution furnished by his own words. This answers the objection, that if he knew of the resurrection in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>, and future retribution (<reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>), why did he not draw his reasonings elsewhere from them, which he did not? God's righteous government, however, needs to be vindicated as to this life also, and therefore the Holy Ghost has caused the argument mainly to turn on it at the same time giving glimpses of a future fuller vindication of God's ways.<div eID="gen7240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought forth--</hi>not "carried away safe" or "escape" (referring to this life), as Umbreit has it.<div eID="gen7241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath--</hi>literally, "wraths," that is, multiplied and fierce wrath. <div eID="gen7242" type="x-p"/>
entries.4facdb8da5be2127bbb69791d7673a16e3eaa6c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4925"/><div sID="gen7243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4925"/>31. That is, who dares to charge him openly with his bad ways? namely, in this present life. He shall, I grant (<reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>), be "repaid" hereafter. <div eID="gen7243" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bc6a7777cf8bc536853e350f85f94177457f01e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4926"/><div sID="gen7244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4926"/><hi type="bold">32. Yet--</hi>rather, "and."<div eID="gen7244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought--</hi>with solemn pomp (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">Psa 45:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grave--</hi>literally, "graves"; that is, the place where the graves are.<div eID="gen7246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remain in--</hi>rather, watch on the tomb, or sepulchral mound. Even after death he seems still to live and watch (that is, have his "remembrance" preserved) by means of the monument over the grave. In opposition to Bildad (<reference osisRef="Job.18.17">Job 18:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7247" type="x-p"/>
entries.d04e21be9e6d332ae4d0b32fce5d9b9f2cd75213: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4927"/><div sID="gen7248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4927"/>33. As the classic saying has it, "The earth is light upon him." His repose shall be "sweet."<div eID="gen7248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw--</hi>follow. He shall share the common lot of mortals; no worse off than they (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">He 9:27</reference>). Umbreit not so well (for it is not true of "every man"). "Most men follow in his bad steps, as countless such preceded him." <div eID="gen7249" type="x-p"/>
entries.51525937427f555ecb1a9432f040c445b11b5446: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4928"/><div sID="gen7250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4928"/><hi type="bold">34. falsehood--</hi>literally, "transgression." Your boasted "consolations" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference>) are contradicted by facts ("vain"); they therefore only betray your evil intent ("wickedness") against me. <chapter eID="Job.21"/>

entries.5a4a52c7c05d0955a970d87b108d966a0d84ebed: <div eID="gen16904" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16905" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16906" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16906" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16905" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16907" type="x-p"/> Job expresses himself as puzzled by the dispensations of Divine Providence, because of the unequal distribution of temporal goods; he shows that wicked men often live long, prosper in their families, in their flocks, and in all their substance, and yet live in defiance of God and sacred things, vv. 1-16. At other times their prosperity is suddenly blasted, and they and their families come to ruin, <reference osisRef="Job.21.17-Job.21.21">Job 21:17-21</reference>. God, however, is too wise to err; and he deals out various lots to all according to his wisdom: some come sooner, others later, to the grave: the strong and the weak, the prince and the peasant, come to a similar end in this life; but the wicked are reserved for a day of wrath, <reference osisRef="Job.21.22-Job.21.33">Job 21:22-33</reference>. He charges his friends with falsehood in their pretended attempts to comfort him, <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">Job 21:34</reference>.
entries.db7aa7485a4d354984a8b8f6dd332df50744c95c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16908" type="x-p"/> Let this be your consolations - ותהי זאת תנחומתיכם uthehi zoth tanchumotheychem may be translated, "And let this be your retractations." Let what I am about to say induce you to retract what you have said, and to recall your false judgments. נחם nacham signifies, not only to comfort, but to change one's mind, to repent; hence the Vulgate translates et agite paenitentiam, "and repent," which Coverdale follows in his version, and amende yourselves. Some suppose the verse to be understood ironically: I am now about to give you consolations for those you have given me. When I have done, then turn them into mockery if you please.
entries.a817b9521d68dfebf7a02e314278d0426040561e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16909" type="x-p"/> As for me - האנכי heanochi, "Alas for me!" Is it not with a man that I speak? And, if this be the case, why should not my spirit be troubled? I do not reply against my Maker: I suffer much from God and man; why then may I not have the privilege of complaining to creatures like myself?
entries.17e2b7e21624730a3e5c40ff3a9874b4d896b8ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16910" type="x-p"/> Mark me, and be astonished - Consider and compare the state in which I was once, with that in which I am now; and be astonished at the judgments and dispensations of God. You will then be confounded; you will put your hands upon your mouths, and keep silent. Putting the hand on the mouth, or the finger on the lips, was the token of silence. The Egyptian god Harpocrates, who was the god of silence, is represented with his finger compressing his upper lip.
entries.c1e0ebf348d113b0b25f23ebe2f107c9ad003f4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16911" type="x-p"/> I am afraid - I am about to speak of the mysterious workings of Providence; and I tremble at the thought of entering into a detail on such a subject; my very flesh trembles.
entries.2c375dca1f7427ebb4d424be56d7f1758b386ea9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16912" type="x-p"/> Wherefore do the wicked live - You have frequently asserted that the wicked are invariably punished in this life; and that the righteous are ever distinguished by the strongest marks of God's providential kindness; how then does it come that many wicked men live long and prosperously, and at last die in peace, without any evidence whatever of God's displeasure? This is a fact that is occurring daily; none can deny it; how then will you reconcile it with your maxims?
entries.a0749e334ed890438975d245a5da1b7ea166f520: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16913" type="x-p"/> Their seed is established - They see their own children grow up, and become settled in the land; and behold their children's children also; so that their generations are not cut off. Even the posterity of the wicked continue.
entries.559c20f43c89518d183f67de0b690855e7e4fdba: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16914" type="x-p"/> Neither is the rod of God upon them - They are not afflicted as other men.
entries.3552cadd4d78b1f198ab3a55e856f3b9934c9085: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16915" type="x-p"/> Their bull gendereth - עבר ibbar, passes over, i.e., on the cow, referring to the actions of the bull when coupling with the female. Their flocks multiply greatly, they bring forth in time, and none of them is barren.
entries.0ccd812e541eb43564fd7d2a58b1d9d41f24d0cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16916" type="x-p"/> They send forth their little ones - It is not very clear whether this refers to the young of the flocks or to their children. The first clause may mean the former, the next clause the latter; while the young of their cattle are in flocks, their numerous children are healthy and vigorous, and dance for joy.
entries.585a902e459fbf6acc6b858c03e512c88f8af028: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16917" type="x-p"/> They take the timbrel and harp - ישאו yisu, they rise up or lift themselves up, probably alluding to the rural exercise of dancing. תף toph, which we translate timbrel, means a sort of drum, such as the tom-tom of the Asiatics. כנור kinnor may mean something of the harp kind. עוגב ugab, organ, means nothing like the instrument now called the organ, though thus translated both by the Septuagint and Vulgate; it probably means the syrinx, composed of several unequal pipes, close at the bottom, which when blown into at the top, gives a very shrill and lively sound. To these instruments the youth are represented as dancing joyfully. Mr. Good translates: "They trip merrily to the sound of the pipe." And illustrates his translation with the following verse: - "Now pursuing, now retreating,Now in circling troops they meet; <div eID="gen16917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16918" type="x-p"/> To brisk notes in cadence beating,Glance their many twinkling feet." <div eID="gen16918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16919" type="x-p"/> The original is intended to convey the true notion of the gambols of the rustic nymphs and swains on festival occasions, and let it be observed that this is spoken of the children of those who say unto God, "Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have if we pray unto him?" <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job 21:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.21.15">Job 21:15</reference>. Is it any wonder that the children of such parents should be living to the flesh, and serving the lusts of the flesh? for neither they nor their parents know God, nor pray unto him.
entries.cfaa622d1c9b55b81b448c17585822e927ef73e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16920" type="x-p"/> They spend their days in wealth - There is a various reading here of some importance. In the text we have יבלו yeballu, they grow old, or wear out as with old age, terent vetustate; and in the margin, יכלו yechallu, they consume; and the Masora states that this is one of the eleven words which are written with ב beth and must be read with כ caph. Several editions have the former word in the text, and the latter in the margin; the former being what is called the kethib, the latter keri. יבלו yeballu, they grow old, or wear out, is the reading of the Antwerp, Paris, and London Polyglots; יכלו yechallu, they accomplish or spend, is the reading of the Complutensian Polyglot, thirteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., the Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic. The Vulgate has ducunt, "they lead or spend," from which our translation is borrowed. I incline to the former, as Job's argument derives considerable strength from this circumstance; they not only spend their days in faring sumptuously every day; but they even wear out so as to grow old in it; they are not cut off by any sudden judgment of God. This is fact; therefore your doctrine, that the wicked are cut off suddenly and have but a short time, is far from the truth. <div eID="gen16920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16921" type="x-p"/> In a moment go down to the grave - They wear out their years in pleasure; grow old in their gay and giddy life; and die, as in a moment, without previous sickness; or, as Mr. Good has it, They quietly descend into the grave.
entries.5f1bd2975e321acd268dc92c9b2fc91384af0b67: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16922" type="x-p"/> They say unto God - This is the language of their conduct, though not directly of their lips. <div eID="gen16922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16923" type="x-p"/> Depart from us - Let us alone; we do not trouble thee. Thy ways are painful; we do not like cross-bearing. Thy ways are spiritual; we wish to live after the flesh. We have learned to do our own will; we do not wish to study thine.
entries.5fe035f784d2d2b70a970b3d1e336f5b45c71cde: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16924" type="x-p"/> What is the Almighty - What allegiance do we owe to him? We feel no obligation to obey him; and what profit can we derive from prayer? We are as happy as flesh and blood can make us: our kingdom is of this world; we wish for no other portion than that which we have. Those who have never prayed as they ought know nothing of the benefits of prayer.
entries.0b434dafaade6c4200396886f8443e4051873453: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16925" type="x-p"/> Their good is not in their hand - With all their boasting and self-dependence, God only lends them his bounty; and though it appears to be their own, yet it is at his disposal. Some of the wicked he permits to live and die in affluence, provided it be acquired in the ordinary way of his providence, by trade, commerce, etc. Others he permits to possess it for a while only, and then strips them of their illegally procured property. <div eID="gen16925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16926" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the wicked is far from me - Some understand the words thus: "Far be it from me to advocate the cause of the wicked." I have nothing in common with them, and am not their apologist. I state a fact: they are often found in continual prosperity. I state another fact: they are often found in wretchedness and misery.
entries.fd963d3ab883ad52b90e45144a244493f7923d6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16927" type="x-p"/> How oft is the candle of the wicked put out? - The candle or lamp is often used, both as the emblem of prosperity and of posterity. Oftentimes the rejoicing of the wicked is short; and, not unfrequently, his seed is cut off from the earth. The root is dried up, and the branch is withered. <div eID="gen16927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16928" type="x-p"/> God distributeth sorrows in his anger - He must be incensed against those who refuse to know, serve, and pray unto him. In his anger, therefore, he portions out to each his due share of misery, vexation, and wo.
entries.da56852466e63144ab0b951168d9c9fed905a1ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16929" type="x-p"/> They are as stubble before the wind - "His fan is in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his floor, and the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, but shall be like the chaff which the wind driveth away." Were not this a common thought, I should have supposed that the author of this book borrowed it from <reference osisRef="Psa.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>. The original signifies that they shall be carried away by a furious storm; and borne off as booty is by the swift-riding robbers of the desert, who make a sudden irruption, and then set off at full speed with their prey.
entries.5d8cec5135c0ca8159b5cb63ba2e1090df60a1b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16930" type="x-p"/> God layeth up his iniquity for his children - This is according to the declaration of God, <reference osisRef="Exo.20.5">Exo 20:5</reference> : "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me." This always supposes that the children, who are thus visited, have copied their parents' example; or that ill-gotten property is found in their hands, which has descended to them from their wicked fathers; and of this God, in his judgments, strips them. It is, however, very natural to suppose that children brought up without the fear of God will walk in the sight of their own eyes, and according to the imaginations of their own hearts. <div eID="gen16930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16931" type="x-p"/> He rewardeth him, and he shall know it - He shall so visit his transgressions upon him, that he shall at last discern that it is God who hath done it. And thus they will find that there would have been profit in serving him, and safety in praying unto him. But this they have neglected, and now it is too late.
entries.82cf34d4c7e5d32741ca042f985c87bb3a79a084: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16932" type="x-p"/> His eyes shall see his destruction - He shall perceive its approach, and have the double punishment of fearing and feeling; feeling a Thousand deaths in fearing One. <div eID="gen16932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16933" type="x-p"/> He shall drink of the wrath - The cup of God's wrath, the cup of trembling, etc., is frequently expressed or referred to in the sacred writings, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.33">Deu 32:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.22">Isa 51:17-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jer 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.8">Rev 14:8</reference>. It appears to be a metaphor taken from those cups of poison which certain criminals were obliged to drink. A cup of the juice of hemlock was the wrath or punishment assigned by the Athenian magistrates to the philosopher Socrates.
entries.748ccbc1c7d8fff045498c705a5caea26fb8ba67: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16934" type="x-p"/> For what pleasure hath he in his house after him - What may happen to his posterity he neither knows nor cares for, as he is now numbered with the dead, and numbered with them before he had lived out half his years. Some have translated the verse thus: "Behold how speedily God destroys the house of the wicked after him! How he shortens the number of his months!"
entries.81f84f32b3740f6f70cd6474643a06d78edb8ae7: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16935" type="x-p"/> Shall any teach God knowledge? - Who among the sons of men can pretend to teach God how to govern the world, who himself teaches those that are high - the heavenly inhabitants, that excel us infinitely both in knowledge and wisdom? Neither angels nor men can comprehend the reasons of the Divine providence. It is a depth known only to God.
entries.e74d9c51a7f0bc93ee5f6929dc52ded6e354223d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16936" type="x-p"/> One dieth in his full strength - In this and the three following verses Job shows that the inequality of fortune, goods, health, strength, etc., decides nothing either for or against persons in reference to the approbation or disapprobation of God, as these various lots are no indications of their wickedness or innocence. One has a sudden, another a lingering death; but by none of these can their eternal states be determined.
entries.019c3e2d84b569bd25050cc4a3f2180a0a14b9b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16937" type="x-p"/> His breasts are full of milk - The word עטיניו atinaiv, which occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, is most likely an Arabic term, but probably so provincial as to be now lost. (Arabic) atana signifies to macerate hides so as to take off the hair: hence Mr. Good thinks it means here, that sleekness of skin which is the effect of fatness both in man and beast. But as the radical idea signifies to stink, as leather does which is thus macerated, I cannot see how this meaning can apply here. Under the root עטן atan, Mr. Parkhurst gives the following definitions:" עטן occurs, not as a verb, but as a noun masculine plural, in construction, עטיני atiney, the bowels, intestines; once <reference osisRef="Job.21.24">Job 21:24</reference>, עטיניו atinaiv, his bowels or intestines, are full of, or abound with, חלב chalab, fat. So the lxx.: Τα δε εγκατα αυτου πληρη στεατος. The Vulgate: Viscera, ejus plena sent adipe, 'his intestines are full of fat.' May not עטינים atinim be a noun masculine plural from עטה atah, to involve, formed as גליונים gailyonim, mirrors, from גלה galah, to reveal? And may nor the intestines, including those fatty parts, the mesentery and omentum, be so called on account of their wonderful involutions?" I think this conjecture to be as likely as any that has yet been formed.
entries.f33dcc5f544928b5659d5a7021ccf34eb943af1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16938" type="x-p"/> They shall lie down alike in the dust - Death levels all distinctions, and the grave makes all equal. There may be a difference in the grave itself; but the human corpse is the same in all. Splendid monuments enshrine corruption; but the sod must lie close and heavy upon the putrefying carcass, to prevent it from becoming the bane of the living.
entries.3d42f3557cad2466ba1331f5f5ef948725d10b28: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16939" type="x-p"/> I know your thoughts - Ye still think that, because I am grievously afflicted, I must therefore be a felonious transgressor.
entries.a3e34eded25cab762ecdc23c725cd0f37c415d59: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16940" type="x-p"/> For ye say, Where is the house of the prince? - In order to prove your point, ye ask, Where is the house of the tyrant and oppressor? <div eID="gen16940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16941" type="x-p"/> Are they not overthrown and destroyed? And is not this a proof that God does not permit the wicked to enjoy prosperity?
entries.bb819d3207aca0dcae53340580dc8b0dcd25b42d: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16942" type="x-p"/> Have ye not asked them that go by the way? - This appears to be Job's answer. Consult travelers who have gone through different countries; and they will tell you that they have seen both examples - the wicked in great prosperity in some instances, while suddenly destroyed in others. See at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">Job 21:34</reference> (note). <div eID="gen16942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16943" type="x-p"/> Do ye not know their tokens - Mr. Good translates the whole verse thus: "Surely thou canst never have inquired of men of travel; or thou couldst not have been ignorant of their tokens. Hadst thou made proper inquiries, thou wouldst have heard of their awful end in a thousand instances. And also of their prosperity." See at the end of this chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">Job 21:34</reference> (note).
entries.6bb8431650465e8e3d09f5ea192a669eca912517: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen16943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16944" type="x-p"/> That the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction? - Though every one can tell that he has seen the wicked in prosperity, and even spend a long life in it; yet this is no proof that God loves him, or that he shall enjoy a prosperous lot in the next world. There, he shall meet with the day of wrath. There, the wicked shall be punished, and the just rewarded.
entries.08fb21fdcd0f8a744405dfc2321ece9df2f051aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen16944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16945" type="x-p"/> Who shall declare his way to his face? - But while the wicked is in power, who shall dare to tell him to his face what his true character is? or, who shall dare to repay him the evil he has done? As such a person cannot have his punishment in this life, he must have it in another; and for this the day of wrath - the day of judgment, is prepared.
entries.1d7bb6622994f97983b2aa390d6867b1f5d20304: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen16945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16946" type="x-p"/> Yet shall he be brought to the grave - He shall die like other men; and the corruption of the grave shall prey upon him. Mr. Carlyle, in his specimens of Arabic poetry, Translations, p. 16, quotes this verse, which he translates and paraphrases, והוא לקברות יובל "He shall be brought to the grave," ועל גדוש ישקוד And shall watch upon the high-raised heap." It was the opinion of the pagan Arabs, that upon the death of any person, a bird, by them called Manah, issued from the brain, and haunted the sepulcher of the deceased, uttering a lamentable scream. <div eID="gen16946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16947" type="x-p"/> This notion, he adds, is evidently alluded to in <reference osisRef="Job.21.32">Job 21:32</reference>. Thus Abusahel, on the death of his mistress: - "If her ghost's funereal screech <div eID="gen16947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16948" type="x-p"/> Through the earth my grave should reach, <div eID="gen16948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16949" type="x-p"/> On that voice I loved so well <div eID="gen16949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16950" type="x-p"/> My transported ghost would dwell."
entries.57776bff4f4afce0eb4d92af1efe4f86b9dafd55: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen16950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16951" type="x-p"/> The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him - Perhaps there is an allusion here to the Asiatic mode of interment for princes, saints, and nobles: a well-watered valley was chosen for the tomb, where a perpetual spring might be secured. This was intended to be the emblem of a resurrection, or of a future life; and to conceal as much as possible the disgrace of the rotting carcass. <div eID="gen16951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16952" type="x-p"/> Every man shall draw after him - There seem to be two allusions intended here: <div eID="gen16952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16953" type="x-p"/> 1. To death, the common lot of all. Millions have gone before him to the tomb; and כל אדם col adam, all men, shall follow him: all past generations have died, all succeeding generations shall die also. <div eID="gen16953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16954" type="x-p"/> 2. To pompous funeral processions; multitudes preceding, and multitudes following, the corpse.
entries.d2122bd331b2a7dadf04799f8a9ec709f37435c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen16954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16955" type="x-p"/> How then comfort ye me in vain - Mr. Good translates: "How vainly then would ye make me retract!" See the note on <reference osisRef="Job.21.2">Job 21:2</reference>. I cannot retract any thing I have said, as I have proved by fact and testimony that your positions are false and unfounded. Your pretensions to comfort me are as hollow as the arguments you bring in support of your exceptionable doctrines. <div eID="gen16955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16956" type="x-p"/> This chapter may be called Job's triumph over the insinuated calumnies, and specious but false doctrines, of his opponents. The irritability of his temper no longer appears: from the time he got that glorious discovery of his Redeemer, and the Joyous hope of an eternal inheritance, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>, etc., we find no more murmurings, nor unsanctified complainings. He is now full master of himself; and reasons conclusively, because he reasons coolly. Impassioned transports no longer carry him away: his mind is serene; his heart, fixed; his hope, steady; and his faith, strong. Zophar the Naamathite is now, in his presence, as an infant in the gripe of a mighty giant. Another of these pretended friends but real enemies comes forward to renew the attack with virulent invective, malevolent insinuation, and unsupported assertion. Him, Job meets, and vanquishes by pious resignation and fervent prayer. Though, at different times after this, Job had his buffetings from his grand adversary, and some seasons of comparative darkness, yet his faith is unshaken, and he stands as a beaten anvil to the stroke. He effectually exculpates himself, and vindicates the dispensations of his Maker. <div eID="gen16956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16957" type="x-p"/> There appears to be something in the <reference osisRef="Job.21.29">Job 21:29</reference> which requires to be farther examined: Have ye not asked them that go by the way? And do ye not know their tokens? It is probable that this verse may allude to the custom of burying the dead by the way-side, and raising up specious and descriptive monuments over them. Job argues that the lot of outward prosperity fell alike to the just and to the unjust, and that the sepulchral monuments by the wayside were proofs of his assertion; for his friends, as well as himself and others, had noted them, and asked the history of such and such persons, from the nearest inhabitants of the place; and the answers, in a great variety of cases, had been: "That monument points out the place where a wicked man lies, who was all his lifetime in prosperity and affluence, yet oppressed the poor, and shut up the bowels of his compassion against the destitute; and this belongs to a man who lived only to serve his God, and to do good to man according to his power, yet had not a day of health, nor an hour of prosperity; God having given to the former his portion in this life, and reserved the recompense of the latter to a future state." <div eID="gen16957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16958" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint render the verse thus: - Ερωτησατε παραπορευμενους ὁδον, και τα σημεια αυτων ουκ απαλλοτριωσατε, "Inquire of those who pass by the way, and their signs [monuments] ye will not alienate." That is, When ye hear the history of these persons, ye will not then assert that the man who lived in prosperity was a genuine worshipper of the true God, and therefore was blessed with temporal good, and that he who lived in adversity was an enemy to God and was consequently cursed with the want of secular blessings. Of the former ye will hear a different account from those who dare now speak the truth, because the prosperous oppressor is no more; And of the latter ye shall learn that, though afflicted, destitute, and distressed, he was one of those who acknowledged God in all his ways, and never performed an act of religious service to him in hope of secular gain; sought his approbation only, and met death cheerfully, in the hope of being eternally with the Lord. <div eID="gen16958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16959" type="x-p"/> Neither good nor evil can be known by the occurrences of this life. Every thing argues the certainty of a future state, and the necessity of a day of judgment. They who are in the habit of marking casualties, especially if those whom they love not are the subjects of them, as tokens of Divine displeasure, only show an ignorance of God's dispensations, and a malevolence of mind that would fain arm itself with the celestial thunders, in order to transfix those whom they deem their enemies.  <chapter eID="Job.21"/> <div eID="gen16959" type="x-p"/>

entries.964774ea3ef015aeb36e6fb53eedfb4f0b2b49ae: <reference osisRef="Job.21.1-Job.6.1">Job 21:1-6   1</reference>  Then began Job, and said:   2  Hear, oh hear, my speech, <div eID="gen7761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7762" type="x-p"/> And let this be instead of your consolations.   3  Suffer me, and I will speak, <div eID="gen7762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7763" type="x-p"/> And after I have spoken thou mayest mock.   4  As for me, then, doth my complaint concern man, <div eID="gen7763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7764" type="x-p"/> Or wherefore should I not become impatient?   5  Turn ye to me and be astonished, <div eID="gen7764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7765" type="x-p"/> And lay your hand upon your mouth.   6  Even if I think of it I am bewildered, <div eID="gen7765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7766" type="x-p"/> And my flesh taketh hold on trembling - : <div eID="gen7766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7767" type="x-p"/> The friends, far from being able to solve the enigma of Job’s affliction, do not once recognise the mystery as such. They cut the knot by wounding Job most deeply by ever more and more frivolous accusations. Therefore he entreats them to be at least willing to listen (שׁמעוּ with the gerund) to his utterance (מלּה) respecting the unsolved enigma; then (<hi type="italic">Waw apodosis imper.</hi>) shall this attention supply the place of their consolations, i.e., be comforting to him, which their previous supposed consolations could not be. They are to bear with him, i.e., without interruption allow him to answer for himself (שׂאוּני with <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> before the tone, as <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.12">Jon 1:12</reference>, comp. קחהוּ,   1Ki 20:33, not as Hirz. thinks under the influence of the distinctive accent, but according to the established rule, Ges. §60, rem. 1); then he will speak (אנכי contrast to the “ye” in שׂאוני without further force), and after he has expressed himself they may mock. It is, however, not תלעיגוּ (as Olshausen corrects), but תלעיג (in a voluntative signific. = תלעג), since Job here addresses himself specially to Zophar, the whole of whose last speech must have left the impression on him of a bitter sarcasm (sarkasmo’s from sarka'zein in the sense of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.19.22">Job 19:22</reference></hi>), and has dealt him the freshest deep blow. In <reference osisRef="Job.21.4">Job 21:4</reference> שׂיחת is not to be understood otherwise than as in <reference osisRef="Job.7.13">Job 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.27">Job 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference>, and is to be translated “my complaint.” Then the prominently placed אנכי is to be taken, after <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.17">Eze 33:17</reference>, Ges. §121, 3, as an emphatic strengthening of the “my”: he places his complaint in contrast with another. This emphasizing is not easily understood, if one, with Hupf., explains: <hi type="italic">nonne hominis est querela mea,</hi> so that ה is equivalent to הלא (which here in the double question is doubly doubtful), and ל is the sign of the cause. Schultens and Berg, who translate לאדם <hi type="italic">more humano,</hi> explain similarly, by again bringing their suspicious ל <hi type="italic">comparativum</hi><note placement="foot">In the passage from Ibn-Kissaï quoted above, p. 421, Schultens, as Fleischer assures me, has erroneously read Arab. <hi type="italic">lmchâlı̂b</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">kmchâlı̂b</hi>, having been misled by the frequent failing of the upper stroke of the Arab. <hi type="italic">k</hi>, and in general Arab. <hi type="italic">l</hi> is never = <hi type="italic">k</hi>, and also ל never = כ, as has been imagined since Schultens.</note> here to bear upon it. The ל by שׂיחי (if it may not also be compared with <reference osisRef="Job.12.8">Job 12:8</reference>) may certainly be expected to denote those to whom the complaint is addressed. We translate: As for me, then, does my complaint concern men? The אנכי which is placed at the beginning of the sentence comes no less under the rule, Ges. §145, 2, than §121, 3. In general, sufferers seek to obtain alleviation of their sufferings by imploring by words and groans the pity of sympathizing men; the complaint, however, which the three hear from him is of a different kind, for he has long since given up the hope of human sympathy, - his complaint concerns not men, but God (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.16.20">Job 16:20</reference>).<note placement="foot">An Arabian proverb says: “The perfect patience is that which allows no complaint to be uttered <hi type="italic">ila el - chalq</hi> against creatures (men).”</note> <div eID="gen7767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7768" type="x-p"/> He reminds them of this by asking further: or (ואם, as <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.9">Job 40:9</reference>, not: and if it were so, as it is explained by Nolde contrary to the usage of the language) why (interrogative upon interrogative: <hi type="italic">an quare,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>, אם הלא, an nonne) should not my spirit (disposition of mind, θυμός) be short, i.e., why should I not be short-tempered (comp. Jdg 10:16; Zec 11:8, with Prov. 13:29) = impatient? Dürr, in his <hi type="italic">commentatio super voce</hi> רוּח,   1776, 4, explains the expression <hi type="italic">habito simul halitus, qui iratis brevis esse solet, respectu,</hi> but the signification breath is far from the nature of the language here; רוח signifies emotional excitement (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.15.13">Job 15:13</reference>), either long restrained (with ארך), or not allowing itself to be restrained and breaking out after a short time (קצר). That which causes his vexation to burst forth is such that the three also, if they would attentively turn to him who thus openly expresses himself, will be astonished and lay their hand on their mouth (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.29.9">Job 29:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.4">Job 40:4</reference>), i.e., they must become dumb in recognition of the puzzle, - a puzzle insoluble to them, but which is nevertheless not to be denied. השׁמו is found in Codd. and among grammarians both as <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. השׁמּוּ <hi type="italic">hashammu</hi> (Kimchi) and as <hi type="italic">Hoph.</hi> השּׁמּוּ, or what is the same, השּׁמּוּ <hi type="italic">hoshshammu</hi> (Abulwalid) with the sharpening of the first radical, which also occurs elsewhere in the <hi type="italic">Hoph.</hi> of this verb (Lev 26:34.) and of others (Olsh. §259, b, 260). The pointing as <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. (השׁמּוּ for השׁמּוּ) in the signification <hi type="italic">obstupescite</hi> is the better attested. Job himself has only to think of this mystery, and he is perplexed, and his flesh lays hold on terror. The expression is like Job 18:20. The emotion is conceived of as a want arising from the subject of it, which that which produces it must as of necessity satisfy. <div eID="gen7768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7769" type="x-p"/> In the following strophe the representation of that which thus excites terror begins. The divine government does not harmonize with, but contradicts, the law maintained by the friends.
entries.4f5c2b524274371082a62535c93a36908bf4b5c3: <reference osisRef="Job.21.7-Job.11.7">Job 21:7-11   7</reference>  Wherefore do the wicked live, <div eID="gen7769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7770" type="x-p"/> Become old, yea, become mighty in power?   8  Their posterity is established before them about them, <div eID="gen7770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7771" type="x-p"/> And their offspring before their eyes.   9  Their houses have peace without fear, <div eID="gen7771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7772" type="x-p"/> And the rod of Eloah cometh not upon them. 10  His (the evil-doer’s) bull gendereth and faileth not; <div eID="gen7772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7773" type="x-p"/> His cow calveth easily, and casteth not her calf. 11  They let their little ones run about as a flock, <div eID="gen7773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7774" type="x-p"/> And their children jump about. <div eID="gen7774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7775" type="x-p"/> The question in <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">Job 21:7</reference> is the same as that which Jeremiah also puts forth, <reference osisRef="Job.12.1">Job 12:1</reference>-3. It is the antithesis of Zophar’s thesis, <reference osisRef="Job.20.5">Job 20:5</reference>, and seeks the reason of the fact established by experience which had also well-nigh proved the ruin of Asaph (Ps 73: comp. Mal 3:13-15), viz., that the ungodly, far from being overtaken by the punishment of their godlessness, continued in the enjoyment of life, that they attain to old age, and also a proportionately increasing power and wealth. The verb עתק, which in <reference osisRef="Job.14.18">Job 14:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference> (comp. the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. <reference osisRef="Job.9.5">Job 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.32.15">Job 32:15</reference>), we read in the signification <hi type="italic">promoveri,</hi> has here, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">‛ataqa , ‛atuqa ,</hi> the signification to become old, <hi type="italic">aetate provehi;</hi> and גּבר חיל, to become strong in property, is a synonym of השׂגּה חיל, to acquire constantly increasing possessions, used in a similar connection in Psa 73:12. The first feature in the picture of the prosperity of the wicked, which the pang of being bereft of his own children brings home to Job, is that they are spared the same kind of loss: their posterity is established (נכון, <hi type="italic">constitutus</hi>, elsewhere standing in readiness, <reference osisRef="Job.12.5">Job 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">Job 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>, here standing firm, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.93.2">Psa 93:2</reference>) in their sight about them (so that they have to mourn neither their loss by death nor by separation from their home), and their offspring (צאצאים, a word common only to the undisputed as well as to the disputed prophecies of Isaiah and the book of Job) before their eyes; נכון must be carried over to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.8">Job 21:8</reference></hi> as predicate: they are, without any loss, before their eyes. The description passes over from the children, the corner-stones of the house (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes., s.v.</hi> בנה), to the houses themselves. It is just as questionable here as in <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">Job 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.3">Isa 41:3</reference>, and elsewhere, whether שׁלום is a subst. (= בשׁלום) or an adj.; the substantival rendering is at least equally admissible in such an elevated poetic speech, and the plur. subject בּתּיהם, which, if the predicate were intended to be taken as an adj., leads one to expect שׁלומים, decides in its favour. On מפּחד, without (far from) terrifying misfortune, as <reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">Isa 22:3</reference>, מקשׁת, without a bow, vid., on Job 19:26. The matter does not admit of one’s deriving the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. יהתּוּ here, as <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job 39:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.34">Job 31:34</reference>, from the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. of the verb חתת, <hi type="italic">terrore percelli;</hi> it is to be referred to נחת or נחת (Aram. for ירד), which is the only certain example of a Hebrew verb <hi type="italic">Pe Nun</hi> ending with ת, whose <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ינחת, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>, also יחת (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.10">Pro 17:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference>), instead of יחת, and in the inflexion its ת sti  (after the analogy of יצּתּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Isa 33:12</reference>) is doubled; as an exception (vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, ii. 468), the lengthening of the short vowel (יחתוּ, Olsh. §83 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) by <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi> does not take place, as e.g., by Athnach, Job 34:5. <div eID="gen7783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7784" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. ויּאמרוּ, in which <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job 21:14</reference> is continued, does not here denote temporally that which follows upon and from something else, but generally that which is inwardly connected with something else, and even with that which is contradictory, and still occurring at the same time, exactly as <reference osisRef="Gen.19.9">Gen 19:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.8">2Sa 3:8</reference>, comp Ew. §231, <hi type="italic">b</hi>: they sink down after a life that is completely consumed away, without a death-struggle, into Hades, and yet they denied God, would not concern themselves about His sways (comp. the similar passage, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">Isa 58:2</reference>), and accounted the service of God and prayer (פּגע בּ, <hi type="italic">precibus adire</hi>) as useless. The words of the ungodly extend to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.15">Job 21:15</reference></hi>; according to Hirz., Hlgst., Welte, and Hahn, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference></hi> resumes the description: behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? i.e., is it not at their free disposal? or do they not everywhere carry it away with them? But <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference></hi> is not favourable to this interrogative rendering of לא (= הלא). Schlottm. explains more correctly: behold, their prosperity is not in their power; but by taking not only <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference></hi> (like Schnurrer), but the whole of <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>, as an utterance of an opponent, which is indeed impossible, because the declining of all fellowship with the godless would be entirely without aim in the mouth of the opponent. For it is not the fnends who draw the picture of the lot of the punishment of the godless with the most terrible lines possible, who suggest the appearance of looking wishfully towards the godless, but Job, who paints the prosperity of the godless in such brilliant colours. On the other hand, both sides are agreed in referring prosperity and misfortune to God as final cause. And for this very reason Job thinks that בּרך את־האלהים, which he makes the godless, in <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job 21:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.21.15">Job 21:15</reference>, express in their own words, so horrible.<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference></hi> is therefore to be taken as Job’s judgment, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference></hi> as the moral effect which it produces upon him. הן introduces the true relation of things, טוּבם signifies, as <reference osisRef="Job.20.21">Job 20:21</reference>, their prosperity, and לא בידם (the emphatic position of בידם is to be observed) that this is not in <hi type="italic">their</hi> hand, i.e., arbitrary power, or perhaps better: that it is not by their own hand, i.e.,that it is not their own work but a gift from above, the gift even of the God whom they so shamelessly deny. That God grants them such great and lasting prosperity, is just the mystery which Job is not able to bring forth to view, without, however, his abhorrence of this denying of God being in the slightest degree lessened thereby. Not by their own hand, says he, do they possess such prosperity - the counsel    (עצת similar to <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.3">Job 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">Job 18:7</reference> : design, principle, and general disposition, or way of thinking) of the wicked be far from me, i.e., be it far from me that so I should speak according to their way of thinking, with which, on the contrary, I disavow all fellowship. The relation of the clauses is exactly like <reference osisRef="Job.22.18">Job 22:18</reference>, where this formula of detesation is repeated. רחקה is, according to the meaning, optative or precative (Ew. §223, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and Ges. §126, 4*), which Hahn and Schlottm. think impossible, without assigning any reason. It is the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. of certainty, which expresses that which is wished as a fact, but with an emotional exclamative accent. In ancient Arabic it is a rule to use the perf. as optative; and also still in modem Arabic (which often makes use of the fut. matead of the perf.), they say e.g., <hi type="italic">la cân</hi>, i.e., he must never have been!
