entries.d9ebb1e220731941453eb9d286f5c686a419fd9c: <reference osisRef="Job.21.17-Job.21.17">Job 21:17-21 17</reference>  How rarely is the light of the wicked put out, <div eID="gen7784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7785" type="x-p"/> And their calamity breaketh in upon them, <div eID="gen7785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7786" type="x-p"/> That He distributeth snares in his wrath, 18  That they become as straw before the wind, <div eID="gen7786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7787" type="x-p"/> And as chaff which the storm sweepeth away!? 19  “Eloah layeth up his iniquity for his children!” <div eID="gen7787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7788" type="x-p"/> May He recompense it to him that he may feel it. 20  May his own eyes see his ruin, <div eID="gen7788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7789" type="x-p"/> And let him drink of the glowing wrath of the Almighty. 21  For what careth he for his house after him, <div eID="gen7789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7790" type="x-p"/> When the number of his months is cut off? <div eID="gen7790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7791" type="x-p"/> The interrogative כּמּה has here the same signification as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference> : how often (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.7.19">Job 7:19</reference>, how long? <reference osisRef="Job.13.23">Job 13:23</reference>, how many?), but in the sense of “how seldom?!” How seldom does what the friends preach to him come to pass, that the lamp of the wicked is put out (thus Bildad, <reference osisRef="Job.13.5">Job 13:5</reference>), and their misfortune breaks in upon them (יבא, <hi type="italic">ingruit;</hi> thus Bildad, <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference> : misfortune, איד, prop. pressure of suffering, stands ready for his fall), that He distributes (comp. Zophar’s ”this is the portion of the wicked man,” i.e., what is allotted to him, <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference>) snares in His wrath. Hirz., Ew., Schlottm., and others, translate הבלים, after the precedent of the Targ. (עדבין, <hi type="italic">sortes</hi>), "lots,” since they understand it, after <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, of visitations of punishment allotted, and as it were measured out with a measuring-line; but that passage is to be translated, “the measuring-lines have fallen to me in pleasant places,” and indeed חבל can signify the land that is allotted to one (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.14">Jos 17:14</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Josh.17.5">Jos 17:5</reference>); but the plural does not occur in that tropical sense, and if it were so intended here, חבליהם or חבלים להם might at least be expected. Rosenm., Ges., Vaih., and Carey transl. with lxx and Jer. (ὠδῖνες, <hi type="italic">dolores</hi>) “pains,” but הבלים is the peculiar word for the writhings of those in travail (<reference osisRef="Job.39.3">Job 39:3</reference>), which is not suited here. Schnurr. and Umbr. are nearer to the correct interpretation when they understand חבלים like פחים, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>, of lightning, as it were fiery strings cast down from above. If we call to mind in how many ways Bildad, <reference osisRef="Job.18.8-Job.18.10">Job 18:8-10</reference>, has represented the end of the godless as a divinely decreed seizure, it is certainly the most natural, with Stick. and Hahn, to translate (as if it were Arabic <hi type="italic">ḥabâ'ilin</hi>) “snares,” to be understood after the idea, however, not of lightning, but generally of ensnaring destinies (e.g., חבלי עני, <reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7792" type="x-p"/> Both <reference osisRef="Job.21.17">Job 21:17</reference> with its three members and <reference osisRef="Job.21.18">Job 21:18</reference> with two, are under the control of כמה. The figure of straw, or rather chopped straw (Arab. <hi type="italic">tibn , tabn</hi>), occurs only here. The figure of chaff is more frequent, e.g., Psa 1:4. Job here puts in the form of a question what <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6">Psa 1:1-6</reference> maintains, being urged on by Zophar’s false application and superficial comprehension of the truth expressed in the opening of the Psalter. What next follows in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.19">Job 21:19</reference></hi> is an objection of the friends in vindication of their thesis, which he anticipates and answers; perhaps the clause is to be spoken with an interrogative accent: Eloah will - so ye object - reserve his evil for his children? אונו, not from און, strength, wealth, as <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">Job 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.10">Job 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.16">Job 40:16</reference>, but from און, wickedness (<reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>) and evil (<reference osisRef="Job.15.35">Job 15:35</reference>), here (without making it clear which) of wickedness punishing itself by calamity, or of calamity which must come forth from the wickedness as a moral necessity comp. on Job 15:31. That this is really the opinion of the friends: God punishes the guilt of the godless, if not in himself, at least in his children, is seen from <reference osisRef="Job.20.10">Job 20:10</reference>; Job 5:4. Job as little as Ezekiel, ch. 18, disputes the doctrine of retribution in itself, but that imperfect apprehension, which, in order that the necessary satisfaction may be rendered to divine justice, maintains a transfer of the punishment which is opposed to the very nature of personality and freedom: may He recompense him himself, וידע, that he may feel it, i.e., repent (which would be in Arab. in a similar sense, <hi type="italic">faja'lamu; </hi>ידע as <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference>; Hos 9:7; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.14">Eze 25:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7793" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference> continues in the same jussive forms; the ἅπ. γεγρ. כּיד signifies destruction (prop. a thrust, blow), in which sense the Arab. <hi type="italic">caid</hi> (commonly: cunning) is also sometimes used. The primary signification of the root כד, Arab. <hi type="italic">kd</hi>, is to strike, push; from this, in the stems Arab. <hi type="italic">kâd , med.</hi> <hi type="italic">Wau</hi> and <hi type="italic">med. Je ,</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">kdd , kdkd ,</hi> the most diversified turns and applications are developed; from it the signif. of כּידוד, <reference osisRef="Job.41.11">Job 41:11</reference>, כּידון, <reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference>, and according to Fleischer (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, pp. 388) also of כּידור, are explained. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference></hi>, as <reference osisRef="Ps.60.5">Psa 60:5</reference>; Oba 1:16, refers to the figure of the cup of the wrath of God which is worked out by Asaph, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.9">Psa 75:9</reference>, and then by the prophets, and by the apocalyptic seer in the New Testament. The emphasis lies on the signs of the person in עינו (עיניו) and ישׁתּה. The rather may his own eyes see his ruin, may he himself have to drink of the divine wrath; for what is his interest (what interest has he) in his house after him? מה puts a question with a negative meaning (hence Arab. <hi type="italic">mâ</hi> is directly used as <hi type="italic">non</hi>); חפץ, prop. inclination, corresponds exactly to the word “interest” (<hi type="italic">quid ejus interest</hi>), as <reference osisRef="Job.22.3">Job 22:3</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa 58:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Isa 58:13</reference> (following his own interest), without being weakened to the signification, affair, πραγμα, a meaning which does not occur in our poet or in Isaiah. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference></hi> is added as a circumstantial clause to the question in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference></hi>: while the number of his own months ... , and the predicate, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">Job 15:20</reference> (which see), is in the plur. <hi type="italic">per attractionem.</hi> Schnurr., Hirz., Umbr., and others explain: if the number of his months is drawn by lot, i.e., is run out; but חצץ as <hi type="italic">v. denom.</hi> from חץ morf, in the signification to shake up arrows as sticks for drawing lots (Arab. <hi type="italic">sahm</hi>, an arrow and a lot, just so Persian <hi type="italic">tı̂r</hi>) in the helmet or elsewhere (comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.26">Eze 21:26</reference>), is foreign to the usage of the Hebrew language (for מחצצים, Jdg 5:11, signifies not those drawing lots, but the archers); besides, חצּץ (<hi type="italic">pass</hi>. חצּץ) would signify “to draw lots,” not “to dispose of by lot,” and “disposed of by lot” is an awkward metaphor for “run out.” Cocceius also gives the choice of returning to חצץ, ψῆφος, in connection with this derivation: <hi type="italic">calculati sive ad calculum,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">pleno numero egressi, </hi>which has still less ground. Better Ges., Ew., and others: if the number of his months is distributed, i.e., to him, so that he (this is the meaning according to Ew.) can at least enjoy his prosperity undisturbed within the limit of life appointed to him. By this interpretation one misses the לו which is wanting, and an interpretation which does not require it to be supplied is therefore to be preferred. All the divers significations of the verbs חצץ (to divide, whence <reference osisRef="Prov.30.27">Pro 30:27</reference>, חצץ, forming divisions, i.e., in rank and file, <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. to shoot with the arrow, Talm. to distribute, to halve, to form a partition), חצה (to divide, <reference osisRef="Job.40.20">Job 40:20</reference>; to divide in two equal parts), Arab. <hi type="italic">hṣṣ</hi> (to divide, whence Arab. <hi type="italic">hṣṣah , portio</hi>), and Arab. <hi type="italic">chṣṣ</hi> (to separate, particularize) - to which, however, Arab. <hi type="italic">chṭṭ</hi> (to draw, write), which Ew. compares here, does not belong - are referable to the primary signification scindere, to cut through, split (whence חץ, an arrow, lxx <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.20">1Sa 20:20</reference>, σχίζα); accordingly the present passage is to be explained: when the number of his months is cut off (Hlgst., Hahn), or cut through, i.e., when a bound is set to the course of his life at which it ends (comp. בּצּע, of the cutting off of the thread of life, <reference osisRef="Job.6.9">Job 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job 27:8</reference>, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣrm</hi>). Job 14:21., <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ecc 3:22</reference>, are parallels to Job 21:21. Death is the end of all clear thought and perception. If therefore the godless receives the reward of his deeds, he should receive it not in his children, but in his own body during life. But this is the very thing that is too frequently found to be wanting.
entries.073fca931e6d3760fa5afcb4b4049c156c3ac6e4: Job 21:22-26 22  Shall one teach God knowledge, <div eID="gen7793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7794" type="x-p"/> Who judgeth those who are in heaven? 23  One dieth in his full strength, <div eID="gen7794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7795" type="x-p"/> Being still cheerful and free from care. 24  His troughs are full of milk, <div eID="gen7795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7796" type="x-p"/> And the marrow of his bones is well watered. 25  And another dieth with a sorrowing spirit, <div eID="gen7796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7797" type="x-p"/> And hath not enjoyed wealth. 26  They lie beside one another in the dust, <div eID="gen7797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7798" type="x-p"/> And worms cover them both. <div eID="gen7798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7799" type="x-p"/> The question, <reference osisRef="Job.21.22">Job 21:22</reference>, concerns the friends. Since they maintain that necessarily and constantly virtue is rewarded by prosperity, and sin by misfortune, but without this law of the divine order of the world which is maintained by them being supported by experience: if they set themselves up as teachers of God, they will teach Him the right understanding of the conduct which is to be followed by Him as a ruler and judge of men, while nevertheless He is the Absolute One, beneath whose judicial rule not merely man, but also the heavenly spirits, are placed, and to which they must conform and bow. The verb למּד, instead of being construed with two acc., as in the dependent passage <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">Isa 40:14</reference>, is here construed with the <hi type="italic">dat</hi>. of the person (which is not to be judged according to <reference osisRef="Job.5.2">Job 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference>, but according to διδάσκειν τινί τι, to teach one anything, beside the other prevailing construction). With והוא a circumstantial clause begins regularly: while He, however, etc. Arnh. and Löwenth. translate: while, however, He exaltedly judges, i.e., according to a law that infinitely transcends man; but that must have been מרום (and even thus it would still be liable to be misunderstood). Hahn (whom Olsh. is inclined to support): but He will judge the proud, to which first the circumstantial clause, and secondly the parallels, <reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Isa 24:21</reference>), from which it is evident that רמים signifies the heavenly beings (as <reference osisRef="Ps.78.69">Psa 78:69</reference>, the heights of heaven), are opposed: it is a fundamental thought of this book, which abounds in allusions to the angels, that the angels, although exalted above men, are nevertheless in contrast with God imperfect, and therefore are removed neither from the possibility of sin nor the necessity of a government which holds them together in unity, and exercises a judicial authority over them. The rule of the all-exalted Judge is different from that which the three presumptuously prescribe to Him. <div eID="gen7799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7800" type="x-p"/> The one (viz., the evil-doer) dies בּעצם תּמּו, <hi type="italic">in ipsa sua integritate, </hi>like בעצם היום, <hi type="italic">ipso illo die;</hi> the Arabic would be <hi type="italic">fı̂ ‛yn ,</hi> since there the eye, here the bone (comp. Uhlemann, <hi type="italic">Syr. Gramm.</hi> §58), denote corporeality, duration, existence, and therefore identity. תּם is intended of perfect external health, as elsewhere מתם; comp. תּמימים, Pro 1:12. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.23">Job 21:23</reference></hi> the pointing שׁלאנן (<hi type="italic">adj.</hi>) and שׁלאנן (3 <hi type="italic">praet.</hi>) are interchanged in the Codd.; the following verbal adjective favours the form of writing with <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>. As to the form, however (which Röd. and Olsh. consider to be an error in writing), it is either a mixed form from שׁאנן and שׁלו with the blended meaning of both (Ew. §106, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), to which the comparison with שׁליו (= שׁלו) is not altogether suitable, or it is formed from שׁאנן by means of an epenthesis (as זלעף from זעף, <hi type="italic">aestuare</hi>, and בלסם, βάλσαμον, from בשׂם), and of similar but intensified signification; we prefer the latter, without however denying the real existence of such mixed forms (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.25">Job 33:25</reference>). This fulness of health and prosperity is depicted in Job 21:24. The ancient translators think, because the bones are mentioned in the parallel line, עטיניו must also be understood of a part of the body: lxx ἔγκατα, Jer. <hi type="italic">viscera;</hi> Targ. בּיזוי, his breasts, βυζία<note placement="foot">Vid., <hi type="italic">Handschriftliche Funde,</hi> 2. S. V.</note> (for Hebr. שׁדים, שׁד); Syr. version <hi type="italic">gabauh</hi> (= <hi type="italic">ganbauh</hi>), his sides in regard to עטמא, Syr. <hi type="italic">‛attmo</hi> = אטמא, side, hip; Saad. <hi type="italic">audâguhu</hi>, his jugular veins, in connection with which (not, however, by this last rendering) חלב is read instead of חלב: his bowels, etc., are full of fat.<note placement="foot">Gesenius in his <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. corrects the אודאגה which was found in Saadia’s manuscript translation to אודאעה, Arab. <hi type="italic">awdâ‛uhu ,</hi> which is intended to mean <hi type="italic">repositoria ejus,</hi> but is really not Arabic; whereas אודאגה is the correct <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. of Arab. <hi type="italic">wadaj :</hi> his jugular veins, which occurs not merely of horses, but also of animals and men. Saadia, with reference to the following מלאוּ חלב, has thought of the metaphorical phrase Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥalaba awdâjahu :</hi> “he has milked his jugular vein,” i.e., he has, as it were, drawn the blood from his jugular veins = <hi type="italic">eum jugulavit ,</hi> vid., <hi type="italic">Bibliotheca Arabo-Sicula,</hi> p. 563: “and with the freshly milked juice of the jugular veins, viz., of the enemy (Arab. <hi type="italic">w - mn ḥlb 'l - 'wdâj</hi>), our infant ready to be weaned is nourished in the midst of the tumult of battle, as soon as he is weaned.” The meaning of Saadia’s translation is then: his jugular veins are filled with fresh blood swollen with fulness of blood. - Fl.</note> <div eID="gen7800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7801" type="x-p"/> But the assumption that עטיניו must be a part of the body is without satisfactory ground (comp. against it e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>, and for it <reference osisRef="Job.20.11">Job 20:11</reference>); and Schlottm. very correctly observes, that in the contrast in connection with the representation of the well-watered marrow one expects a reference to a rich nutritious drink. To this expectation corresponds the translation: “his resting-places (i.e., of his flocks) are full of milk,” after the Arab. <hi type="italic">‛aṭan</hi>or <hi type="italic">ma‛ṭin</hi>. which was not first compared by Schultens and Reiske (<hi type="italic">epaulia</hi>), but even by Abul-walid, Aben-Ezra, and others. <div eID="gen7801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7802" type="x-p"/> But since the reference of what was intended to be said of the cattle at the watering-places to the places where the water is, possesses no poetic beauty, and the Hebrew language furnished the poet with an abundance of other words for pastures and meadows, it is from the first more probable that עטיניו are large troughs, - like Talm. מעטן, a trough, in which the unripe olives were laid in order that they might become tender and give forth oil, that they may then be ready for the oil-press (בּד), and עטן denotes this laying in itself, - and indeed either milk-tubs or milk-pails (שׁחולבין לתוכן), or with Kimchi (who rightly characterizes this as more in accordance with the prosperous condition which is intended to be described), the troughs for the store of milk, which also accords better with the meaning of the verb עטן, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛aṭana</hi>, to lay in, <hi type="italic">confire</hi>.<note placement="foot">The Arab. verb <hi type="italic">'tn</hi>, compared by the Orientals themselves with Arab. <hi type="italic">wtn</hi>, cognate in sound and meaning, has the primary signification to lie secure and to lay secure, as Arab. <hi type="italic">'atan</hi>, a resting-place of camels, sheep, and goats about the watering-places, is only specifically distinct from Arab. <hi type="italic">watan,</hi> a cow-shed, cow-stall. The common generic notion is always a resting-place, wherefore the Kamus interprets <hi type="italic">'attan</hi> by <hi type="italic">wattan wa-mebrek,</hi> viz., round about the drinking-places. Arab. <hi type="italic">ma'tin</hi> as <hi type="italic">n. loci</hi>, written <hi type="italic">m'atén</hi> by Barth in his <hi type="italic">Wanderungen durch die Küstenländer des Mittelmeeres,</hi> Bd. i. (vid., <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenländ. Zeitschrift,</hi> iv. S. 275) S. 500, 517, is similar in meaning. The Arab. verb <hi type="italic">'atana, impf. j'attunu,</hi> also <hi type="italic">j'attina, n. act. 'uttûn, a v. instrans.,</hi> signifies, viz., of camels, etc., to lay themselves down around the drinking-troughs, after or even before drinking from them. On the other hand, Arab. <hi type="italic">'atana, impf. j'attinu,</hi> also <hi type="italic">j'attunu, n. act. 'attn,</hi> a <hi type="italic">v. trans.</hi> used by the dresser of skins: to lay the skins in the tan or ooze (French, <hi type="italic">confire;</hi> low Latin, <hi type="italic">tanare, tannare,</hi> whence French, <hi type="italic">tanner,</hi> to tan, <hi type="italic">tan,</hi> the bark) until they are ready for dressing, and the hairs will easily scrape off. Hence Arab. <hi type="italic">'atina, impf. j'attanu, n. act. 'attan,</hi> a <hi type="italic">v. intrans.</hi> used of skins: to become tender by lying in the ooze, and to smell musty, to stink, which is then transferred to men and animals: to stink like a skin in the ooze, comp. situs, mould, mildew, rest. - Fl. Starting from the latter signification, <hi type="italic">macerare pellem,</hi> Lee explains: his bottles (viz., made of leather); and Carey: his half-dressed skins (because the store of milk is so great that he cannot wait for the preparation of the leather for the bottles); but the former is impossible, the latter out of taste, and both are far-fetched.</note> <div eID="gen7802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> From the abundance of nutriment in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.24">Job 21:24</reference></hi>, the description passes over in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.24">Job 21:24</reference></hi> to the well-nourished condition of the rich man himself in consequence of this abundance. מח (Arab. <hi type="italic">muchch</hi>, or even <hi type="italic">nuchch</hi>, as נף = מף, <hi type="italic">naurag</hi> = מורג) is the marrow in the bones, e.g., the spinal marrow, but also the brain as the marrow of the head (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 233). The bones (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>), or as it is here more exactly expressed, their marrow, is watered, when the body is inwardly filled with vigour, strength, and health; Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Isa 58:11</reference>, fills up the picture more (as a well-watered garden), and carries it still further in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa 66:14</reference> (thy bones shall blossom like a tender herb). The counterpart now follows with וזה (and the other, like <reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>). The other (viz., the righteous) dies with a sorrowful soul (comp. Job’s lament, <reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference>), i.e., one which is called to experience the bitterness of a suffering life; he dies and has not enjoyed בּטּובה, any of the wealth (with partitive <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Psa 141:4</reference>, comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.13">Job 7:13</reference>), has had no portion in the enjoyment of it (comp. Job’s lament, <reference osisRef="Job.9.25">Job 9:25</reference>). In death they are then both, unrighteous and righteous, alike, as the Preacher said: מקרה אחד comes upon the wise as upon the fool, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.15">Ecc 2:15</reference>, comp. Job 9:2. They lie together in the dust, i.e., the dust of the grave (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>), and worms cover them. What then is become of the law of retribution in the present world, which the friends maintained with such rigid pertinacity, and so regardless of the deep wound they were inflicting on Job?
entries.74a449c51ed7a04efbac902f648ce85ee1dc1930: Job 21:27-31 27  Behold I know your thoughts <div eID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7804" type="x-p"/> And the stratagems, with which ye overpower me! 28  When ye say: Where is the house of the tyrant, <div eID="gen7804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> And where the pavilions of the wicked - : 29  Have ye not asked those who travel, <div eID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> Their memorable things ye could surely not disown: 30  That the wicked was spared in the day of calamity, <div eID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> In the day of the outburst of wrath they were led away. 31  Who liketh to declare to him his way to his face? <div eID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> And hath he done aught, who will recompense it to him? <div eID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> Their thoughts which he sees through, are their secret thoughts that he is such an evil-doer reaping the reward of his deeds. מזמּות (which occurs both of right measures, good wise designs, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.12">Pro 8:12</reference>, and of artful devices, malicious intrigues, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.17">Pro 14:17</reference>, comp. the definition of בּעל מזמּות, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.8">Pro 24:8</reference>) is the name he gives to the delicately developed reasoning with which they attack him; חמס (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">taḥammasa</hi>, to act harshly, violently, and overbearingly) is construed with על in the sense of forcing, apart from the idea of overcoming. In <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference>, which is the antecedent to <reference osisRef="Job.21.29">Job 21:29</reference>, beginning with כּי האמרוּ (as <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>), he refers to words of the friends like <reference osisRef="Job.8.22">Job 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.34">Job 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.15">Job 18:15</reference>, Job 18:21. נדיב is prop. the noble man, whose heart impels (נדב, Arab. <hi type="italic">nadaba</hi>) him to what is good, or who is ready and willing, and does spontaneously that which is good (Arab. <hi type="italic">naduba</hi>), vid., Psychol. S. 165; then, however, since the notion takes the reverse way of generosus, the noble man (princely) by birth and station, with which the secondary notion of pride and abuse of power, therefore of a despot or tyrant, is easily as here (parall. רשׁעים, comp. עשׁיר, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa 53:9</reference>, with the same word in the parallel) combined (just so in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Isa 13:2</reference>, and similarly at least above, <reference osisRef="Job.12.21">Job 12:21</reference>, - an anomaly of name and conduct, which will be for the future put aside, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa 32:5</reference>). It is not admissible to understand the double question as antithetical, with Wolfson, after <reference osisRef="Prov.14.11">Pro 14:11</reference>; for the interrogative איּה is not appropriate to the house of the נדיב, in the proper sense of the word. <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference>, משׁכנות is not an externally but internally multiplying plur.; perhaps the poet by byt intends a palace in the city, and by אהל משׁכנות a tent among the wandering tribes, rendered prominent by its spaciousness and the splendour of the establishment.<note placement="foot">Although the tents regularly consist of two divisions, one for the men and another for the women, the translation “magnificent pavilion” (<hi type="italic">Prachtgezelt</hi>), disputed by Hirz., is perfectly correct; for even in the present day a Beduin, as he approaches an encampment, knows the tent of the sheikh immediately: it is denoted by its size, often also by the lances planted at the door, and also, as is easily imagined, by the rich arrangement of cushions and carpets. Vid., Layard’s <hi type="italic">New Discoveries</hi>, pp. 261 and 171.</note> <div eID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> Job thinks the friends reason a <hi type="italic">priori</hi> since they inquire thus; the permanent fact of experience is quite different, as they can learn from ערי דרך, travellers, i.e., here: people who have travelled much, and therefore are well acquainted with the stories of human destinies. The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> נכּר, proceeding from the radical meaning to gaze fixedly, is an enantio'seemon, since it signifies both to have regard to, <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job 34:19</reference>, and to disown, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.27">Deu 32:27</reference>; here it is to be translated: their אתת ye cannot nevertheless deny, ignore (as Arab. <hi type="italic">nakira</hi> and <hi type="italic">ankara</hi>). אתת are tokens, here: remarkable things, and indeed the remarkable histories related by them; Arab. <hi type="italic">âyatun</hi> (collective plur. <hi type="italic">âyun</hi>), signs, is also similarly used in the signification of Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ibrat</hi>, example, historical teaching. <div eID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> That the כּי, <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference>, introduces the view of the friends, and is the antecedent clause to <reference osisRef="Job.21.31">Job 21:31</reference> : <hi type="italic">quod </hi>(<hi type="italic">si</hi>) <hi type="italic">vos dicitis, in tempora cladis per iram divinam immissae servari et nescium futuri velut pecudem eo deduci improbum</hi> (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">de fin.</hi> §76), has in the double ל an apparent support, which is not to be denied, especially in regard to <reference osisRef="Job.38.23">Job 38:23</reference>; it is, however, on account of the omission of the indispensable תאמרו in this instance, an explanation which does violence to the words. The כּי, on the contrary, introduces that which the accounts of the travellers affirm. Further, the ל in ליום indicates here not the <hi type="italic">terminus ad quem,</hi> but as in לערב, in the evening, the <hi type="italic">terminus quo.</hi> And the verb חשׂך, <hi type="italic">cohibere</hi>, signifies here to hold back from danger, as <reference osisRef="Job.33.18">Job 33:18</reference>, therefore to preserve uninjured. Ew. translates <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference></hi> erroneously: “in the day when the floods of wrath come on.” How tame would this הוּבל, “to be led near,” be! This <hi type="italic">Hoph</hi>. signifies elsewhere to be brought and conducted, and occurs in <reference osisRef="Job.21.32">Job 21:32</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Isa 55:12</reference> and elsewhere, of an honourable escort; here, in accordance with the connection: to be led away out of the danger (somewhat as Lot and his family by the escort of angels). At the time, when streams of wrath (עברה, the overflowing of vexation = outburst of wrath, like the Arab. <hi type="italic">‛abrt</hi>, the overflowing of the eye = tears) go forth, they remain untouched: they escape them, as being under a special, higher protection.<note placement="foot">This interpretation, however, is unsatisfactory, because it does not do justice to the twofold ל, which seems, according to <reference osisRef="Job.38.23">Job 38:23</reference>, to be intended to indicate the <hi type="italic">terminus ad quem;</hi> perhaps <reference osisRef="Job.21.29">Job 21:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference> are to be transposed. If <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference> followed <reference osisRef="Job.21.28">Job 21:28</reference>, it would retain its natural sense as belonging to the view of the friends: “For the wicked is reserved for the day of calamity, and to a day of wrath they are led” (יובלו as <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa 53:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jer 11:19</reference>). Then והוא לקברות יובל also adds a suitable echo of the contradiction in Job’s mouth. Böttch. rightly calls attention to the consonance of יובל with יובלו, and of עברות with קברות.</note> <div eID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.21.31">Job 21:31</reference> is commonly taken as a reflection on the exemption of the evil-doer: God’s mode of action is exalted above all human scrutiny, although it is not reconcilable with the idea of justice, <reference osisRef="Job.9.12">Job 9:12</reference>; Job 23:13. But the מי ישׁלּם־לו, who will recompense it to him, which, used of man in relation to God, has no suitable meaning, and must therefore mean: who, after God has left the evil-doer unpunished - for which, however, הוּא עשׂה would be an unsuitable expression - shall recompense him, the evil-doer? is opposed to it. Therefore, against Ew., Hirz., and Hlgst., it must with most expositors be supposed that <reference osisRef="Job.21.31">Job 21:31</reference> is a reflection referable not to God, but to the evil-doer: so powerful is the wicked generally, that no one can oppose his pernicious doings and call him to account for them, much less that any one would venture to repay him according to his desert when he has brought anything to a completion (הוּא עשׂה, intentionally thus seriously expressed, as elsewhere of God, e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">Isa 38:15</reference>). In the next strophe, that which is gathered from the accounts of travellers is continued, and is then followed by a declamatory summing up.
entries.e3114702dc7470b18936431b00a9c9acec541f0e: Job 21:32-34 32  And he is brought to the grave, <div eID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7813" type="x-p"/> And over the tomb he still keepeth watch. 33  The clods of the valley are sweet to him, <div eID="gen7813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7814" type="x-p"/> And all men draw after him, <div eID="gen7814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7815" type="x-p"/> As they preceded him without number. .   .   .   .   .   . 34  And how will ye comfort me so vainly! <div eID="gen7815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7816" type="x-p"/> Your replies are and remain perfidy. <div eID="gen7816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7817" type="x-p"/> During life removed at the time of dire calamity, this unapproachable evil-doer is after his death carried to the grave with all honour (יוּבל, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.10.19">Job 10:19</reference>), and indeed to a splendid tomb; for, like משׁכנות above, קברות is also an amplificative plural. It is certainly the most natural to refer ישׁקד, like יוּבל, to the deceased. The explanation: and over the tomb one keeps watch (Böttch., Hahn, Röd., Olsh.), is indeed in itself admissible, since that which serves as the efficient subject is often left unexpressed (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.2">Gen 48:2</reference>; 2Ki 9:21; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa 53:9</reference>; comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, on <reference osisRef="Job.18.18">Job 18:18</reference>); but that, according to the prevalent usage of the language, ישׁקד would denote only a guard of honour at night, not also in the day, and that for clearness it would have required גּדישׁו instead of גּדישׁ, are considerations which do not favour this explanation, for שׁקד signifies to watch, to be active, instead of sleeping or resting; and moreover, the placing of guards of honour by graves is an assumed, but not proved, custom of antiquity. Nevertheless, ישׁקד might also in general denote the watchful, careful tending of the grave, and the <hi type="italic">maqâm</hi> (the tomb) of one who is highly honoured has, according to Moslem custom, servants (<hi type="italic">châdimı̂n</hi>) who are appointed for this duty. But though the translation “one watches” should not be objected to on this ground, the preference is to be given to a commendable rendering which makes the deceased the subject of ישׁקד. Raschi’s explanation does not, however, commend itself: “buried in his own land, he also in death still keeps watch over the heaps of sheaves.” The lxx translates similarly, ἐπὶ σωρῶν, which Jerome improperly, but according to a right sentiment, translates, <hi type="italic">in congerie mortuorum.</hi> For after the preceding mention of the pomp of burial, גּדישׁ, which certainly signifies a heap of sheaves in <reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>, is favoured by the assumption of its signifying a sepulchral heap, with reference to which also in that passage (where interment is likewise the subject of discourse) the expression is chosen. Haji Gaon observes that the dome (קבּה, Arab. <hi type="italic">qbbt</hi>, the dome and the sepulchral monument vaulted over by it)<note placement="foot">Vid., Lane’s <hi type="italic">Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians</hi> (translated by Zenker).</note> erected over graves according to Arab custom is intended; and Aben-Ezra says, that not exactly this, but in general the grave-mound formed of earth, etc., is to be understood. In reality, גדישׁ (from the verb גדשׁ, <hi type="italic">cumulare,</hi> commonly used in the Talmud and Aramaic) signifies <hi type="italic">cumulus</hi>, in the most diversified connections, which in Arabic are distributed among the verbs <hi type="italic">jds , kds , and jdš ,</hi> especially <hi type="italic">tumulus</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">jadatun</hi> (broader pronunciation <hi type="italic">jadafun</hi>). If by grave-mound a mound with the grave upon it can be understood, a beautiful explanation is presented which accords with the preference of the Beduin for being buried on an eminence, in order that even in death he may be surrounded by his relations, and as it were be able still to overlook their encampment: the one who should have had a better lot is buried in the best place of the plain, in an insignificant grave; the rich man, however, is brought up to an eminence and keeps watch on his elevated tomb, since from this eminence as from a watch-tower he even in death, as it were, enjoys the wide prospect which delighted him so while living.<note placement="foot">“Take my bones,” says an Arabian poem, “and carry them with you, wherever you go; and if ye bury them, bury them opposite your encampment! And bury me not under a vine, which would shade me, but upon a hill, so that my eye can see you!” Vid., <hi type="italic">Ausland</hi>, 1863, Nr. 15 (<hi type="italic">Ein Ritt nach Transjordanien</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen7817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7818" type="x-p"/> But the signification <hi type="italic">collis</hi> cannot be supported; גדישׁ signifies the hill which is formed by the grave itself, and <reference osisRef="Job.21.33">Job 21:33</reference> indeed directs us to the wady as the place of burial, not to the hill. But if גדישׁ is the grave-mound, it is also not possible with Schlottm. to think of the pictures on the wall and images of the deceased, as they are found in the Egyptian vaults (although in <reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job 3:14</reference> we recognised an allusion to the pyramids), for it cannot then be a גדישׁ in the strict sense that is spoken of; the word ought, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">jdṯ</hi> (which the Arab. translation of the New Testament in the London Polyglott uses of the μνημεῖον of Jesus), with a mingling of its original signification, to have been used in the general signification <hi type="italic">sepulcrum</hi>. This would be possible, but it need not be supposed. Job’s words are the pictorial antithesis to Bildad’s assertion, <reference osisRef="Job.18.17">Job 18:17</reference>, that the godless man dies away without trace or memorial; it is not so, but as may be heard from the mouth of people who have experience in the world: he keeps watch over his tomb, he continues to watch although asleep, since he is continually brought to remembrance by the monument built over his tomb. A keeping watch that no one approaches the tomb disrespectfully (Ew.), is not to be thought of. שׁקד is a relative negation of the sleep of death: he is dead, but in a certain manner he continues to live, viz., in the monument planting forward his memory, which it remains for the imagination to conceive of as a mausoleum, or weapons, or other votive offerings hung upon the walls, etc. In connection with such honour, which follows him even to and beyond death, the clods of the valley (<hi type="italic">est ei terra levis</hi>) are sweet (מתקוּ is accentuated with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>, and לו without <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> with little-<hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>) to him; and if death in itself ought to be accounted an evil, he has shared the common fate which all men after him will meet, and which all before him have met; it is the common end of all made sweet to him by the pageantry of his burial and his after-fame. Most modern expositors (Ew., Hirz., Umbr., Hlgst., Welte) understand the ימשׁך, which is used, certainly, not in the transitive signification: to draw after one’s self, but in the intransitive: to draw towards (lxx απελεύσεται), as Jdg 4:6 (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.), of an imitative treading of the same way; but כּל־אדם would then be an untrue hyperbole, by which Job would expose himself to the attack of his adversaries. <div eID="gen7818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7819" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">Job 21:34</reference> Job concludes his speech; the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of ואיך, according to the idea (as e.g., the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> in ואני, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.12">Isa 43:12</reference>), is an inferential <hi type="italic">ergo</hi>. Their consolation, which is only available on condition of penitence, is useless; and their replies, which are intended to make him an evil-doer against the testimony of his conscience, remain מעל. It is not necessary to construe: and as to your answers, only מעל remains. The predicate stands <hi type="italic">per attractionem</hi> in the sing.: their answers, reduced to their true value, leave nothing behind but מעל, end in מעל, viz., באלהים, <reference osisRef="Josh.22.22">Jos 22:22</reference>, perfidious sinning against God, i.e., on account of the sanctimonious injustice and uncharitableness with which they look suspiciously on him. <div eID="gen7819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7820" type="x-p"/> Job has hitherto answered the accusations of the friends, which they express in ever-increasingly terrible representations of the end of the godless, presenting only the terrible side of their dogma of the justice of God, with a stedfast attestation of his innocence, and with the ever-increasing hope of divine vindication against human accusation. In him was manifest that faith which, being thrust back by men, clings to God, and, thrust back by God, even soars aloft from the present wrath of God to His faithfulness and mercy. The friends, however, instead of learning in Job’s spiritual condition to distinguish between the appearance and the reality in this confidence, which comes back to itself, see in it only a constant wilful hardening of himself against their exhortations to penitence. It does not confound them, that he over whom, according to their firm opinion, the sword of God’s vengeance hangs, warns them of that same sword, but only confirms them still more in their conviction, that they have to do with one who is grievously self-deluded. <div eID="gen7820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7821" type="x-p"/> Zophar has painted anew the end of the evil-doer in the most hideous colours, in order that Job might behold himself in this mirror, and be astonished at himself. We see also, from the answer of Job to Zophar’s speech, that the passionate excitement which Job displayed at first in opposition to the friends has given place to a calmer tone; he has already got over the first impression of disappointed expectation, and the more confidently certain of the infallibility of divine justice he becomes, the more does he feel raised above his accusers. He now expects no further comfort; careful attention to what he has to say shall henceforth be his consolation. He will also complain against and of men no more, for he has long since ceased to hope for anything for himself from men; his vexation concerns the objective indefensibility of that which his opponents maintain as a primeval law of the divine government in the world. The maxim that godlessness always works its own punishment by a calamitous issue, is by no means supported by experience. One sees godless persons who are determined to know nothing of God, and are at the same time prosperous. It is not to be said that God treasures up the punishment they have deserved for their children. The godless ought rather to bear the punishment themselves, since the destiny of their children no longer concerns them after they have enjoyed their fill of life. That law is therefore a precept which human short-sightedness has laid down for God, but one by which, however, He is not guided. The godless who have lived prosperously all their days, and the righteous who have experienced only sorrow, share the common lot of death. One has only to ask persons who have had experience of the world: they can relate instances of notorious sinners who maintained their high position until death, and who, without being overtaken by divine judgments, and without human opposition and contradiction, were carried in honour to the grave, and their memory is immortalized by the monuments erected over their tomb. From this Job infers that the connection into which the friends bring his suffering with supposed guilt, is a false one, and that all their answers are, after all, reducible to an unjust and uncharitable judgment, by which they attack (מעל) God. <div eID="gen7821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7822" type="x-p"/> Job has more than once given expression to the thought, that a just distribution of prosperity and misfortune is not to be found in the world, <reference osisRef="Job.9.22-Job.9.24">Job 9:22-24</reference>; Job 12:6. But now for the first time he designedly brings it forward in reply to the friends, after he has found every form of assertion of his innocence unavailing, and their behaviour towards him with their dogma is become still more and more inconsiderate and rash. Job sins in this speech; but in order to form a correct judgment of this sinning, two things must be attended to. Job does not revel in the contradiction in which this lasting fact of experience stands to the justice of divine retribution, he had rather be ignorant of it; for he has no need of it in order, in spite of his affliction, to be able to hold fast the consciousness of his innocence. No indeed! if he thinks of this mystery he is perplexed, and shuddering comes over him, Job 21:6. And when he depicts the prosperity of sinners, he expresses his horror of the sins of such prosperous men in the words: The counsel of the ungodly be far from me! (<reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference>), in order that it may not be erroneously imagined that he lusts after such prosperity. <div eID="gen7822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> If we compare Zophar’s and Job’s speeches one with another, we are obliged to say, that relatively the greater right is on the side of Job. True, the Scriptures confirm what Zophar says of the destruction of the evil-doer in innumerable passages; and this calamitous end of one who has long been prosperous and defiant, is the solution by which the Old Testament Scriptures (Ps. 37, 73; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.3">Jer 12:1-3</reference>; Hab. 1:13-2:1) remove the stumbling-block of the mysterious phenomenon of the prosperity of the evil-doer. But if we bear in mind that this solution is insufficient, so long as that calamitous end is regarded only outwardly, and with reference to the present world, - that the solution only becomes satisfactory when, as in the book of Ecclesiastes, in reply to a similar doubt to that which Job expresses (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ecc 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ecc 8:14</reference>), the end is regarded as the end of all, and as the decision of a final judgment which sets all contradictions right, - that, however, neither Zophar nor Job know anything of a decision beyond death, but regard death as the end whither human destiny and divine retribution tend, without being capable of any further distinction: we cannot deny that Job is most in the right in placing the prosperous life and death of the godless as based upon the incontrovertible facts of experience, in opposition to Zophar’s primeval exceptionless law of the terrible end of the godless. The speeches of Zophar and of Job are both true and false, - both one-sided, and therefore mutually supplementary. The real final end of the evil-doer is indeed none other than Zophar describes; and the temporal prosperity of the evil-doer, lasting often until death, is really a frequent phenomenon. If, however, we consider further, that Job is not able to deny the occurrence of such examples of punishment, such revelations of the retributive justice of God, as those which Zophar represents as occurring regularly and without exception; that, however, on the other hand, exceptional instances undeniably do exist, and the friends <hi type="italic">are obliged</hi> to be blind to them, because otherwise the whole structure of their opposition would fall in, - it is manifest that Job is nearer to the truth than Zophar. For it is truer that the retributive justice of God is often, but by far not always, revealed in the present world and outwardly, than that it never becomes manifest. <div eID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7824" type="x-p"/> Wherein, then, does Job’s sin in this speech consist? Herein, that he altogether ignores the palpably just distribution of human destinies, which does occur frequently enough. In this he becomes unjust towards his opponent, and incapable of convincing him. From it, it appears as though in the divine government there is not merely a preponderance of what is mysterious, of what is irreconcilable with divine justice, but as though justice were altogether contradicted. The reproach with which he reproaches his opponents: Shall one teach God understanding? is one which also applies to himself; for when he says that God, if He punishes, must visit punishment upon the evil-doer himself, and not on his children, it is an unbecoming dictation with regard to God’s doing. We should be mistaken in supposing that the poet, in <reference osisRef="Job.21.19-Job.21.21">Job 21:19-21</reference>, brings forward a concealed contradiction to the Mosaic doctrine of retribution; nowhere in the Old Testament, not even in the Mosaic law, is it taught, that God visits the sins of the fathers on the children, while He allows them themselves to go free, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Exo 20:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.24.16">Deu 24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.1">Eze 18:1</reference>; Jer 31:29. What Job asserts, that the sinner himself must endure the punishment of his sins, not his children instead of him, is true; but the thought lying in the background, that God does not punish where He ought to punish, is sinful. Thus here Job again falls into error, which he must by and by penitently acknowledge and confess, by speaking unbecomingly of God: the God of the future is again vanished from him behind the clouds of temptation, and he is unable to understand and love the God of the present; He is a mystery to him, the incomprehensibility of which causes him pain. “The joyous thought of the future, which a little before struggled forth, again vanishes, because the present, into the abyss of which he is again drawn down, has remained perfectly dark the whole time, and as yet no bridge has been revealed crossing from this side to that.”  <chapter eID="Job.21"/> <div eID="gen7824" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the Grave, which is low and deep like a Valley.</ns0:note> shall be sweet unto him <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He shall sweetly rest in his Grave, free from all cares, and fears, and troubles, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 17, 18.</ns0:note>, and every man shall draw after him <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>He shall draw every man after him,</ns0:hi> to wit, into the Grave, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All that live after him, whether good or bad, shall follow him into the Grave, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> shall dye as he did.                   <ns0:p n="34">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:403" />34. How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
